newsitem.title: GERMANY: No Buba rate move seen, gold debate to top agenda.
newsitem.headline: No Buba rate move seen, gold debate to top agenda.

text.p: This week's Bundesbank council meeting is unlikely to yield a change in interest rates but a heated exchange on the Bonn government's plans to revalue the central bank's assets is expected to take centre stage.

Since German Finance Minister Theo Waigel made an unannounced exit from a debate on European monetary union to fly to the Frankfurt-based Bundesbank two weeks ago, Bonn's plans to raid the bank's treasure chest have provoked a constant stream of comment and criticism.

The minister's unscheduled appearance at a Bundesbank council meeting only hours before the release of data revealing an 18 billion mark ($10.7 billion) shortfall in expected tax revenues led to speculation that his actions were those of a desperate man.

With only seven months of 1997 to go, many economists see little hope that Bonn can rein in its budget deficit to 3 percent of gross domestic product to qualify fairly and squarely for the start of European monetary union in 1999.

Precise details of Waigel's plans for the central bank's gold and reserve assets have not been published. Following preliminary talks with the central bank on May 15 the central bank pledged to draw up a draft paper on its plans.
This week's meeting, which takes place Wednesday because of a holiday on Thursday, will be the first chance for the central bank to discuss the plans since Waigel made his proposal.
Although the central bank will not have the final say in how the revaluation takes place, it will have a strong voice.
The assumption is that the assets, which are currently valued in the central bank's books at their lowest market price, will be raised to somewhere near market levels.
Its gold also is currently valued around 40 billion marks ($23.7 billion) below the current market price, although it is by no means clear the revaluation will be fully to current market levels.
Dutch central bank head Wim Duisenberg, who will take over as the head of the Eurepean Monetary Institute in July, said Monday he had no problem with the German plan.

He told Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper he expected other countries, including Germany, to follow the Dutch model of valuing gold reserves at 70 percent of the average market value over three years.

The plan is being sold as a necessary move to bring the Bundesbank's balance sheet into line with others ahead of the switch to a European central bank, while also neatly reducing Bonn's debt with an, albeit unrealized, windfall profit.

German officials, including Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt have expressed support for the plan in the face of criticism that the move is a dodgy way to raise extra revenue in the run-up to Maastricht.
Rexrodt said in Paris Monday, "My opinion is that we can proceed and should proceed. There is space for such a revaluation and it is a serious measure."
But economists have speculated that the plan has found less favour with the traditionally conservative central bank.
They also feel the apparently last-minute nature of the move reeks of a lack of foresight and planning.

"Whatever happens in this discussion, the general impression is that the German administration is not yet able to structure and implement a rigorous fiscal policy," UBS Global Research said in a commentary.

BHF Bank attacked the principle of paying out unrealized profit: "It may be true that the accounting principles of the EMI council foresee balances in market prices, but unrealized profits from a revaluation may not be used as income."

Sale of the gold to realise the profit is seen as out of the question, particularly in view of vocal German opposition to the International Monetary Fund's plans to sell off just 5 percent of its gold to aid poor countries.

Waigel himself made clear at a news conference on May 15 that he did not plan either to sell the gold or to use the income from the revaluation to cut the budget deficit, which would be at odds with European Union rules.
